questions.question: What is the underlying storage type returned by typeof(42.5) in R?
questions.hint: In R, numeric numbers with decimals are stored internally as 64-bit double-precision floating-point numbers.
questions.explanation: In R, general numeric numbers are stored in double-precision floating-point format. Therefore, typeof(42.5) returns "double", while class(42.5) returns "numeric".

questions.question: How do you instruct R to store the number 25 strictly as an integer data type rather than a double?
questions.hint: Think of the capital letter suffix used historically in languages like C to indicate a Long/integer literal.
questions.explanation: Appending a capital 'L' to a whole number literal (e.g., 25L) forces R to store it as a 32-bit integer in memory. Without 'L', R defaults to storing 25 as a double.

questions.question: What will typeof("100") return in R?
questions.hint: Any value enclosed in quotation marks is treated as text.
questions.explanation: Values enclosed in single or double quotes are treated as character data in R. Even though 100 looks like a number, the quotes make it a text string, so typeof("100") returns "character".

questions.question: If marks <- 75, what is the result and data type of the expression passed <- marks >= 50?
options: Result is 1, data type is integer
Result is TRUE, data type is logical
Result is "TRUE", data type is character
Result is 75, data type is numeric
questions.hint: Relational operators in R evaluate to boolean truth values.
questions.explanation: Comparison operators like >= evaluate to boolean values (TRUE or FALSE). Since 75 >= 50 is true, passed holds TRUE, and typeof(passed) returns "logical".

questions.question: In the complex number z <- 3 + 4i, what does 'i' mathematically represent?
options: The index position in a list
The imaginary unit equal to the square root of -1
questions.hint: Complex numbers consist of a real part plus an imaginary part.
questions.explanation: In R, 'i' represents the imaginary unit sqrt(-1). Complex numbers are used in electrical engineering, physics, and advanced signal processing.

questions.question: What is the key difference between typeof() and class() in R?
options: typeof() and class() are identical aliases and always return the same string
typeof() reveals low-level internal memory storage, while class() indicates high-level object behavior and method dispatch
typeof() only works on numbers, while class() only works on strings
typeof() prints to screen, while class() saves to disk
questions.hint: One tells you how R stores the bytes in RAM, while the other tells you how R treats the object conceptually.
questions.explanation: typeof() reports the low-level C-level internal data representation (e.g., "double", "integer", "character"), whereas class() reports the high-level S3/S4 object class (e.g., "numeric", "Date", "data.frame").

questions.question: What is the exact result of executing as.integer(29.85) in R?
options: NA (decimals cannot be converted to integers)
questions.hint: Integer conversion in R discards the fraction rather than rounding up.
questions.explanation: In R, as.integer() truncates the fractional portion towards zero without rounding. Thus, as.integer(29.85) evaluates strictly to 29L.

questions.question: What happens when you run as.numeric("DataScience") in the R console?
options: NA is returned along with a warning: 'NAs introduced by coercion'
R halts execution with a fatal syntax crash
questions.hint: R cannot parse non-numeric text into a number, so it inserts a missing value indicator.
questions.explanation: When text that does not represent a valid numeral is coerced using as.numeric(), R produces NA and issues a warning: 'NAs introduced by coercion'.

questions.question: How does NULL fundamentally differ from NA in R?
options: NULL represents missing data in a vector, while NA means zero
NULL represents the complete absence of an object or an empty entity, while NA is a placeholder for a missing value within a data type
NULL is used for text, while NA is used only for numbers
There is no difference; they are exact synonyms
questions.hint: Think of NULL as an empty void (nothing exists), whereas NA is a specific missing measurement inside a dataset.
questions.explanation: NULL is an atomic object representing the empty set or absence of an entity. NA represents a missing or unknown value within an existing vector or variable (and has typed variants like NA_character_, NA_integer_, etc.).

questions.question: What is the result of evaluating 0 / 0 in R, and what does is.na(0 / 0) return?
options: Result is Inf, is.na() returns FALSE
Result is NaN (Not a Number), and is.na(NaN) returns TRUE
questions.hint: Zero divided by zero is mathematically indeterminate, and R treats NaN as a special case of missing value.
questions.explanation: 0 / 0 produces NaN (Not a Number). In R, every NaN is also considered a missing value for statistical operations, so is.na(NaN) returns TRUE. However, is.nan(NA) is FALSE.

questions.question: What will 10 / 0 evaluate to in R, and which function confirms its status?
questions.hint: Dividing a positive number by zero yields infinity according to IEEE floating-point standards.
questions.explanation: Dividing a positive non-zero number by zero produces Inf (positive infinity). R implements IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic. You can check it with is.infinite(10 / 0), which returns TRUE.

questions.question: Given exam_marks <- c(80, 90, NA, 70), what does mean(exam_marks) return, and how can you calculate the average of the available scores?
options: Throws an error; you must delete the entire vector
Returns NA; calculate average using mean(exam_marks, na.rm = TRUE)
Returns 60; R automatically assumes NA is 0
questions.hint: Any arithmetic operation with NA propagates NA unless you explicitly instruct R to remove missing values.
questions.explanation: By default, mathematical operations propagate missing values (NA). mean(exam_marks) returns NA. Adding na.rm = TRUE instructs R to ignore missing elements, returning (80 + 90 + 70) / 3 = 80.
